meta.subject: INTEGRATED_3
meta.author: bank-team-integrated-3
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Define a sample space for an experiment
questions.stem: Item 0001 asks a meteorologist to define the sample space for rolling one die.

options.text: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes.
The sample space is only the outcomes that actually occur.
The sample space is the most likely outcome.
options.misconception: reduces space to a single outcome

options.text: The sample space excludes outcomes with probability zero.

questions.explanation: A sample space lists every possible outcome of an experiment, regardless of likelihood.

questions.stem: Item 0002 asks an analyst to review an equally likely outcomes claim.

options.text: Outcomes are equally likely whenever there are two of them.
options.misconception: assumes two outcomes imply equal probability

options.text: Outcomes are equally likely only when symmetry supports it.
Outcomes are equally likely if they are listed alphabetically.
Outcomes are equally likely after observing data.

questions.explanation: Equal likelihood requires physical or logical symmetry, not just the number of categories.

questions.stem: Item 0003 asks a meteorologist to explain non-uniform sample spaces.

answer.exemplar: In a non-uniform sample space, outcomes have different probabilities, so each outcome's probability must be assigned rather than assumed equal.

questions.explanation: Non-uniform spaces require explicit probabilities because symmetry does not justify equal weights.

questions.stem: Item 0004 asks an analyst to count permutations of 6 items taken 2 at a time.
questions.explanation: Permutations count order, so P(6,2) = 6*5 = 30.

questions.stem: Item 0005 asks a meteorologist to find P(A and B) if P(A)=0.2 and P(B)=0.5 and they are independent.
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply: 0.2 * 0.5 = 0.1.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the sign and size of a correlation
questions.stem: Item 0006 asks an analyst to interpret a correlation coefficient r = -0.8.

options.text: There is a strong positive linear relationship.
There is a weak negative linear relationship.
There is a strong negative linear relationship.
Correlation proves one variable causes the other.

questions.explanation: The magnitude 0.8 is strong and the sign is negative, so the linear relationship is strong and negative.
questions.hint: Magnitude gives strength, sign gives direction.

questions.stem: Item 0007 asks a meteorologist to distinguish correlation from causation.

options.text: Causation can only be shown by a sample space.
options.misconception: confuses experimental design with sample space

options.text: A high correlation proves a causal link.
Causation requires a negative correlation.
Correlation alone does not establish causation.

questions.explanation: Correlation measures association; causation requires controlled design or additional evidence.

questions.stem: Item 0008 asks an analyst to review a categorical encoding claim.

options.text: Categorical variables should always be treated as numbers.
Dummy variables encode categories as 0 or 1.
One dummy variable is needed for every category including reference.
Encoding changes the original measurements.

questions.explanation: Dummy variables represent category membership with 0/1 indicators, leaving one reference category.

questions.learningObjective: Identify claims beyond a sample's support
questions.stem: Item 0009 asks a meteorologist to explain unsupported sample claims.

answer.exemplar: A sample supports only claims about the population and conditions it represents, so extrapolating to other groups or times is unsupported.

questions.explanation: Generalising beyond the sampled population or period goes beyond what the data can support.

questions.stem: Item 0010 asks an analyst to compute the standard error when sigma=4 and n=16.
questions.explanation: The standard error is sigma/sqrt(n) = 4/4 = 1.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a joint probability from a tree
questions.stem: Item 0011 asks a meteorologist to find P(cloudy and rain) if P(cloudy)=0.5 and P(rain|cloudy)=0.6.
questions.explanation: Multiply along the branch: 0.5 * 0.6 = 0.3.

questions.stem: Item 0012 asks an analyst to compute P(A|B).

options.text: Divide the joint probability by P(B).
Divide P(B) by the joint probability.
Subtract P(B) from the joint probability.
Multiply P(A) and P(B).

questions.explanation: Conditional probability is P(A and B)/P(B), so divide the joint probability by P(B).

questions.stem: Item 0013 asks a meteorologist to identify binomial parameters.

options.text: The success probability must be 0.5.
Any two outcomes make a binomial distribution.
n independent trials with success probability p.
Trials can depend on each other.

questions.explanation: A binomial model needs a fixed number of independent trials and a constant success probability.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the empirical rule to normal data
questions.stem: Item 0014 asks an analyst to review an empirical rule claim.

options.text: About 68% of values lie within three standard deviations.
About 95% of values lie within one standard deviation.
options.misconception: confuses one and two sigma percentages

options.text: The empirical rule applies to any distribution.
About 95% of values lie within two standard deviations.

questions.explanation: For normal data, roughly 95% fall within two standard deviations of the mean.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Item 0015 asks a meteorologist to explain normal distributions.

answer.exemplar: A normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean, median, and mode equal, and probabilities follow the empirical rule.

questions.explanation: Symmetry and the empirical rule characterise normal distributions and their spread.

questions.learningObjective: Compute standard error of a mean
questions.stem: Item 0016 asks an analyst to compute the standard error when sigma=12 and n=36.
questions.explanation: Standard error = 12/sqrt(36) = 12/6 = 2.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.learningObjective: Define Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Item 0017 asks a meteorologist to compute power if beta=0.2.
questions.explanation: Power is 1 - beta = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8.

questions.stem: Item 0018 asks an analyst to interpret power.

options.text: Power is the probability of rejecting a true null.
options.misconception: confuses power with Type I error

options.text: Power is the probability of rejecting a false null.
Power is the probability of failing to reject a false null.
Power is always 1 regardless of sample size.

questions.explanation: Power is the chance a test correctly rejects the null when the alternative is true.

questions.stem: Item 0019 asks a meteorologist to compute a z-score.

options.text: Divide the value by the mean only.
Subtract the standard deviation and divide by the mean.
Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.
Subtract the median and divide by the range.

questions.explanation: A z-score standardises a value by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.stem: Item 0020 asks an analyst to review a standard error claim.

options.text: Standard error is always zero for large samples.
Standard error is the same as population standard deviation.
options.misconception: confuses sample mean variability with population spread

options.text: Standard error increases as sample size increases.
Standard error measures variability of a sample mean.

questions.explanation: Standard error quantifies how far a sample mean typically varies from the population mean.

questions.stem: Item 0021 asks a meteorologist to explain confidence intervals.

answer.exemplar: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on sample data and a chosen confidence level.

questions.explanation: The interval captures plausible parameter values, not the probability that one specific interval contains the parameter.

questions.stem: Item 0022 asks an analyst to state the common significance threshold alpha.
questions.explanation: A common decision threshold is alpha = 0.05.

questions.learningObjective: Apply Bayes' theorem to a base rate
questions.stem: Item 0023 asks a meteorologist to compute P(disease|positive) if prevalence=0.01, sensitivity=0.99, false positive rate=0.05.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the null hypothesis
questions.stem: Item 0024 asks an analyst to explain the null hypothesis.

options.text: The null is the researcher's hoped-for result.
The null is the default claim tested for evidence against.
The null can be proven true by failing to reject it.
options.misconception: treats failure to reject as proof

options.text: The null is never used in decision making.

questions.explanation: The null represents the default position, and data must provide sufficient evidence against it.

questions.stem: Item 0025 asks a meteorologist to apply a p-value decision rule.

options.text: Never reject if p-value equals 0.5.
Reject the null if p-value is greater than alpha.
Reject the null if p-value is less than alpha.
Reject whenever the sample size is large.

questions.explanation: When the p-value is below alpha, the result is statistically significant and the null is rejected.

questions.stem: Item 0026 asks an analyst to review a residual plot claim.

options.text: Residuals are the same as fitted values.
A curved pattern in residuals suggests nonlinearity.
options.misconception: actually supports nonlinearity, but option says? Wait we need correct A maybe. Let's set A correct and B misconception 'ignores curved pattern'.

options.text: Residuals should increase with fitted values always.
Random scatter suggests the linear model fits well.

questions.explanation: Random scatter around zero indicates the linear model captures the trend adequately.

questions.stem: Item 0027 asks a meteorologist to explain nonlinear relationships.

answer.exemplar: A nonlinear relationship changes at a varying rate, so a straight line cannot capture its trend and a curved model is needed.

questions.explanation: When the rate of change varies, linear fits leave systematic residual patterns.

questions.stem: Item 0028 asks an analyst to compute a residual standard deviation if SSE=100 and n=25.
questions.explanation: sqrt(SSE/n) = sqrt(100/25) = sqrt(4) = 2.

questions.topic: What an analysis of variance tests
questions.stem: Item 0029 asks a meteorologist to compute F if MSbetween=10 and MSwithin=2.
questions.explanation: F = MSbetween / MSwithin = 10 / 2 = 5.

questions.topic: Slope of a line of best fit
questions.learningObjective: Interpret slope of a regression line
questions.stem: Item 0030 asks an analyst to interpret regression slope.

options.text: Slope is the average value of y.
Slope is the predicted change in y per one-unit change in x.
Slope is the correlation coefficient.
Slope is always positive.

questions.explanation: In a linear fit, slope measures the predicted change in response for a one-unit increase in predictor.
questions.hint: Change in y per unit x.

questions.topic: Predictions from a line of best fit
questions.learningObjective: Make a prediction from a regression line
questions.stem: Item 0031 asks a meteorologist to predict from a regression line.

options.text: Predict the mean of y for every x.
Use the correlation coefficient as the prediction.
Substitute the x-value into the fitted equation.
Extrapolate far beyond observed x-values without caution.

questions.explanation: A prediction from the fitted line is obtained by substituting the predictor value into the equation.

questions.stem: Item 0032 asks an analyst to review a residual claim.

options.text: A residual is the correlation coefficient.
A residual is predicted y minus observed y.
A residual is the slope of the fit.
A residual is observed y minus predicted y.

questions.explanation: Residuals measure vertical distance from data point to fitted line as observed minus predicted.

questions.stem: Item 0033 asks a meteorologist to explain correlation computation.

answer.exemplar: Correlation standardises both variables, multiplies paired z-scores, and averages the products to measure linear association.

questions.explanation: Standardising removes units, so the average product of z-scores captures linear association.

questions.learningObjective: Compute an expected count in a two-way table
questions.stem: Item 0034 asks an analyst to compute an expected count if row total=40, column total=50, and grand total=200.
questions.explanation: Expected count = (40*50)/200 = 10.
questions.hint: Multiply totals and divide by grand total.

questions.stem: Item 0035 asks a meteorologist to compute chi-squared if observed=12, expected=10 and observed=8, expected=10.

questions.topic: Updating a probability from a test result
questions.learningObjective: Update a probability after new information
questions.stem: Item 0036 asks an analyst to update a probability after a test result.

options.text: Ignore the prior probability entirely.
Use Bayes' theorem to combine prior and likelihood.
Use only the test's false positive rate.
Add the prior and likelihood.
options.misconception: uses addition instead of Bayes' rule

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem updates the prior probability using the test's likelihoods.

questions.stem: Item 0037 asks a meteorologist to compute binomial standard deviation.

options.text: Use sqrt(n p).
Use n p (1-p).
Use sqrt(n p (1-p)).
Use n p.

questions.explanation: The standard deviation of a binomial count is sqrt(n p (1-p)).

questions.stem: Item 0038 asks an analyst to review a significance claim.

options.text: Only large samples can show practical significance.
options.misconception: ties practical importance to sample size

options.text: A small p-value always means a large effect.
Practical significance requires p > 0.05.
Statistical significance does not imply practical importance.

questions.explanation: A tiny effect can be statistically significant with enough data but still unimportant in practice.

questions.topic: Why the null is the default
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the null is the default
questions.stem: Item 0039 asks a meteorologist to explain why the null is the default.

answer.exemplar: The null is the default because it represents no effect or no difference, and evidence must overcome that baseline before claiming an effect.

questions.explanation: Starting from no effect protects against claiming patterns that could arise by chance.

questions.stem: Item 0040 asks an analyst to compute the margin of error if z=1.96 and SE=2.
questions.explanation: Margin of error = 1.96 * 2 = 3.92.

questions.learningObjective: Count outcomes in a sample space
questions.stem: Item 0041 asks a meteorologist to count outcomes for rolling two dice.
questions.explanation: Each die has 6 faces, so 6*6 = 36 ordered outcomes.

questions.learningObjective: Test equal likelihood in a sample space
questions.stem: Item 0042 asks an analyst to test equal likelihood.

options.text: Equal likelihood follows from having two outcomes.
options.misconception: assumes two outcomes imply equal probability

options.text: Equal likelihood requires symmetric or fair mechanisms.
Equal likelihood follows from alphabetical labels.
Equal likelihood is guaranteed after collecting data.

questions.explanation: Symmetry or fairness justifies equal likelihood; outcome count alone does not.

questions.stem: Item 0043 asks a meteorologist to review a non-uniform claim.

options.text: Non-uniform spaces require equal counts of outcomes.
Non-uniform spaces are impossible in probability.
Non-uniform spaces assign different probabilities to outcomes.
Non-uniform spaces always sum to more than 1.

questions.explanation: Outcomes can have unequal probabilities as long as they sum to 1.

questions.stem: Item 0044 asks an analyst to explain permutations versus combinations.

answer.exemplar: Permutations count arrangements where order matters, while combinations count selections where order does not matter.

questions.explanation: The key distinction is whether rearranging selected items creates a different outcome.

questions.stem: Item 0045 asks a meteorologist to explain independence testing.

answer.exemplar: Two events are independent if P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B), so comparing the joint probability with the product tests independence.

questions.explanation: The multiplication rule provides a direct test for independence.

questions.stem: Item 0046 asks an analyst to compute t if r=0.5 and n=25.
Item 0047 asks a meteorologist to compute r^2 if r=0.8.
questions.explanation: Squaring 0.8 gives 0.64, the proportion of variance explained.

questions.stem: Item 0048 asks an analyst to explain dummy encoding.

options.text: Encoding changes the measured values.
Every category gets its own dummy including reference.
Categories should be coded as consecutive integers.
Dummy variables use 0/1 indicators with one reference category.

questions.explanation: Using 0/1 indicators with one reference avoids redundant columns and perfect collinearity.

questions.stem: Item 0049 asks a meteorologist to review an overgeneralisation claim.

options.text: A sample supports claims about any population.
Sample claims must stay within the sampled population.
Sample size does not affect generalisability.
Convenience samples are always representative.

questions.explanation: A sample supports conclusions about the population it represents, not arbitrary groups.

questions.stem: Item 0050 asks an analyst to explain unchecked assumptions.

answer.exemplar: Some assumptions, such as independence or random sampling, cannot be verified from the data alone and must be justified by design.

questions.explanation: Data cannot prove design assumptions; study design and domain knowledge must support them.

questions.stem: Item 0051 asks a meteorologist to explain probability trees.

answer.exemplar: A probability tree organises sequential events, with branch probabilities multiplied along paths and added across disjoint paths.

questions.explanation: Trees make conditional probabilities explicit and combine them by multiplication and addition.

questions.stem: Item 0052 asks an analyst to compute P(A|B) if P(A and B)=0.2 and P(B)=0.5.
questions.explanation: Divide joint by P(B): 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4.

questions.stem: Item 0053 asks a meteorologist to compute the expected count if n=10 and p=0.3.
questions.explanation: The expected count is n*p = 10*0.3 = 3.

questions.stem: Item 0054 asks an analyst to apply the empirical rule.

options.text: The empirical rule applies to any distribution.
About 95% of normal values lie within one standard deviation.
options.misconception: confuses one and two sigma percentages

options.text: About 95% of normal values lie within two standard deviations.
About 68% of normal values lie within three standard deviations.

questions.explanation: For normal data, roughly 95% fall within two standard deviations of the mean.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Item 0055 asks a meteorologist to review a normal distribution claim.

options.text: Normal distributions have no standard deviation.
A normal distribution is always skewed right.
The mean and median must differ in a normal distribution.
A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean.

questions.explanation: Normal distributions are symmetric, so mean, median, and mode coincide.

questions.learningObjective: Explain sampling distribution of a mean
questions.stem: Item 0056 asks an analyst to explain sampling distributions of a mean.

answer.exemplar: The sampling distribution of the mean describes how sample means vary across repeated samples, with spread measured by standard error.

questions.explanation: Repeated sample means form a distribution whose centre is the population mean and whose spread is the standard error.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.learningObjective: Explain Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Item 0057 asks a meteorologist to explain Type I and Type II errors.

answer.exemplar: A Type I error rejects a true null, while a Type II error fails to reject a false null, and their probabilities trade off.

questions.explanation: The two errors describe opposite mistakes, and reducing one often increases the other.

questions.stem: Item 0058 asks an analyst to compute power if beta=0.2.
Item 0059 asks a meteorologist to compute the z-score if x=110, mu=100, sigma=15.

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.stem: Item 0060 asks an analyst to explain standard error.

options.text: Standard error is sigma times square root of n.
Standard error is sigma divided by square root of n.
Standard error is sigma squared divided by n.
options.misconception: uses variance instead of standard deviation

options.text: Standard error is always zero for large n.

questions.explanation: The standard error of the mean is sigma/sqrt(n), so larger samples reduce it.
